documents.unit: University Policy Register (Office of General Counsel / Provost)
documents.title: 3342-3-01.8 Administrative policy regarding student cheating and plagiarism
documents.date_or_term: current (accessed 2026-10-25); revised to add generative AI
documents.summary: Kent State's binding cheating and plagiarism rule was revised to add generative AI. It defines GAI, bans GAI content on exams and assigned coursework unless the instructor expressly permits it, and folds GAI into the plagiarism definition, then runs it through the existing sanction and hearing process.
documents.stance_why: The document says cheating includes "Using GAI to generate content in satisfaction of assigned coursework, except as expressly permitted by the instructor in the syllabus, or applicable assignment" and bars GAI in exams "except as expressly permitted". AI is banned by default and allowed only where the instructor permits, so restrict rather than delegates, since it sets a default itself.

units.why: The purpose clause says students must work "according to standards set by faculty members, departments, schools and colleges", so standards (including AI rules) are set below the university level. This is a delegation of who decides, so P04 fits better than P56 because it assigns the decision rather than stating a framework.
units.anchor: standards set by faculty members, departments, schools and colleges of the university

units.why: The exam clause makes use of "content generated by internet-based generative artificial intelligence programs (GAI)" in exams, tests and quizzes cheating unless the instructor expressly permits it. It is a ban on AI in assessments with an instructor exception, so P22 fits; P06 (fallback) also touches it but the exam ban is the specific rule.
units.anchor: content generated by internet-based generative artificial intelligence programs (GAI), in examinations, tests and quizzes
units.frag_start: Using notes, textbooks or other information
units.frag_end: the instructor in the syllabus, examination, test, or quiz;

units.why: The exception "except as expressly permitted by the instructor in the syllabus, examination, test, or quiz" lets the instructor lift the exam AI ban through the syllabus or the exam itself. It is a statement of who may permit AI on assessments, so P04 (instructor decides) fits better than P22, which is the ban itself.
units.anchor: except as expressly permitted by the instructor in the syllabus, examination, test, or quiz
units.frag_start: Using notes, textbooks or other information
units.frag_end: the instructor in the syllabus, examination, test, or quiz;

units.why: Coursework clause: "Using GAI to generate content in satisfaction of assigned coursework" is cheating. The default is that GAI-generated submitted work is forbidden, so P19 (do not have AI produce the work you submit) fits.
units.anchor: Using GAI to generate content in satisfaction of assigned coursework

units.why: The coursework ban holds "except as expressly permitted by the instructor in the syllabus, or applicable assignment", so the instructor or assignment sets whether GAI is allowed. This is per-instructor and per-assignment authority, P04. P06 (silent syllabus) is a second fit, but this unit is about who permits.
units.anchor: except as expressly permitted by the instructor in the syllabus, or applicable assignment

units.why: The phrase "except as expressly permitted" means AI is banned unless the instructor says otherwise; the default when the syllabus is silent is prohibition. This fallback rule is P06; P01 is close but the document pairs the default with a required express permission.
units.anchor: except as expressly permitted by the instructor in the syllabus, or applicable assignment
units.policy: Unless the instructor expressly permits it in the syllabus or applicable assignment, using GAI to generate content for assigned coursework is cheating.

units.why: "Presenting data or other material gathered by another person, group, or by GAI, as one's own" is listed as cheating. It bars passing GAI-gathered material off as one's own, which is P29 (own what you submit); P19 is about generating content, whereas this is about misrepresenting authorship.
units.anchor: material gathered by another person, group, or by GAI, as one's own
units.frag_start: Presenting data or other material gathered

units.why: "Having another person, or GAI, take one's place for any academic performance" without the instructor's knowledge and permission is cheating. It forbids GAI substituting for the student unless the instructor knowingly permits it; P19 is the closest type for AI producing the submitted performance.
units.anchor: Having another person, or GAI, take one's place for any academic performance
units.frag_end: knowledge and permission of the instructor;

units.why: The plagiarism definition names GAI as a source: taking and presenting "the ideas or words of another (e.g. person, persons, or GAI)" as one's own is plagiarism. It treats GAI like an outside source under existing plagiarism rules, so P45; P36 covers classification as misconduct but this unit is about the source analogy.
units.anchor: the ideas or words of another (e.g. person, persons, or GAI)
units.frag_end: proper credit to the source of the ideas, words, or works.
units.policy: Plagiarize means to take and present as one's own a material portion of the ideas or words of another (e.g. person, persons, or GAI) without full and proper credit.

units.why: The document classifies GAI misuse under "cheat" and "plagiarize" and says such acts "constitute fraudulent misrepresentation for which no credit can be given and for which appropriate sanctions are warranted and will be applied." That makes unauthorized GAI use academic misconduct handled by integrity sanctions, P36.
units.anchor: no credit can be given and for which appropriate sanctions are warranted
units.frag_start: cheating and plagiarism constitute fraudulent misrepresentation
units.policy: Cheating and plagiarism, which include unauthorized GAI use as defined in the policy, receive no credit and appropriate sanctions are applied.

units.why: The definitions section defines GAI as "internet-based generative artificial intelligence programs that make use of large language model algorithms". This sets what the policy covers, so P61.
units.anchor: internet-based generative artificial intelligence programs that make use of large language model algorithms

units.why: The definition excludes "auto-complete, minor text-predictions, and/or grammar/spelling/punctuation suggestions" in word processors from GAI, so those tools are outside the ban. This scoping of built-in tools fits P07 (AI built into editors); P61 is the general definition but this sentence speaks to embedded tool features specifically.
units.anchor: auto-complete, minor text-predictions, and/or grammar/spelling/punctuation suggestions

units.why: The sanctions section lets the instructor "Refuse to accept the work for credit" or assign "F" or zero for the work or an "F" for the course; since GAI misuse is cheating, these are the penalties for it. Concrete penalties stated in advance, P37.
units.anchor: Assign a grade of "F" or zero for the project, test, paper, examination
units.frag_start: Refuse to accept the work for credit
units.frag_end: Assign a grade of "F" for the course
units.policy: Instructors may refuse to accept the work for credit, assign an F or zero for the work, or assign an F for the course in which cheating or plagiarism took place.

units.why: Degree-level sanctions such as "Rejection of the thesis, dissertation or work" or "Recommendation for revocation of a degree" apply where cheating compromises the validity of a degree. They are escalated penalties stated in advance, P37.
units.anchor: Recommendation for revocation of a degree
units.frag_start: Revocation or recommendation to decertify or not to certify
units.policy: For cheating or plagiarism that compromises the validity of a degree, sanctions include rejection of the thesis, dissertation or work and recommendation for revocation of a degree.

units.why: The AHP section lets the hearing panel assess "disciplinary probation", suspension or dismissal when academic sanctions are insufficient. These are advance-stated escalated penalties, P37.
units.anchor: the offense is of such nature that the academic sanctions are an insufficient remedy
units.frag_start: If the instructor feels, or the department chair
units.frag_end: academic hearing panel defined in paragraph (I) of this rule
units.policy: If academic sanctions are an insufficient remedy or not available, the matter may be referred to the academic hearing panel, which can impose additional disciplinary sanctions such as disciplinary probation, suspension or dismissal.

units.why: The procedure requires an instructor who finds it "more probable than not" that cheating occurred to "Inform the student as soon as is practical". Talking with the student before sanctioning is P57.
units.anchor: Inform the student as soon as is practical of the belief that an act
units.frag_end: the procedural steps the instructor has taken.

units.why: Instructors must "Provide the student an opportunity to explain orally, in writing, or both" why the evaluation is wrong. This gives the accused student a right to respond, P64; P57 is about instructor-student conversation before escalation, but this one is the student's right.
units.anchor: Provide the student an opportunity to explain orally, in writing, or both
units.frag_end: evaluation of the facts is erroneous.

units.why: The hearing rules put the burden on the accuser ("by a preponderance of the evidence") and give the student rights to make a statement, question the instructor, present witnesses and see evidence. These are fairness protections in integrity cases, P64.
units.anchor: Both have the right to hear all testimony and examine all evidence

units.why: Appeals provisions state the student must file "within fifteen working days" and may appeal to the hearing panel and then the provost. These are due-process rights for sanctioned students, including in GAI cases, so P64.
units.anchor: filed with the office of student conduct by the student within fifteen working days
units.frag_start: An appeal of a sanction imposed by an instructor

units.why: "Plagiarism school" offers a remedial session through the libraries to students not previously sanctioned, in return for a mitigated sanction. It is a reduced-consequence route, the nearest type is P38; it is not a self-report window, so this is a loose fit.
units.anchor: attend a remedial, private session administered by university libraries
units.frag_end: regarding acceptable ways to document research.
units.policy: For less severe, unintentional plagiarism by students not previously sanctioned, the instructor may request a remedial private session run by university libraries, after which the sanction is mitigated.

units.why: The instructor "shall keep the evidence of cheating or plagiarism in a secure place" and give it on request to the chair, dean or hearing panel. This is an evidence-handling rule for integrity cases; no type covers evidence retention, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: keep the evidence of cheating or plagiarism in a secure place
units.frag_start: The instructor shall keep the evidence
units.uncovered_note: Instructors must retain and secure evidence of cheating or plagiarism and provide it to chairs, deans, the hearing panel, or the student on request.

units.why: The policy says the AHP "will conduct hearings based on allegations of academic misconduct" with severity and "overall behavior regarding academic honesty" determining sanctions. This is an integrity process covering unauthorized AI use, P36.
units.anchor: The AHP will conduct hearings based on allegations of academic misconduct

units.why: The intent clause says cheating and plagiarism "are serious offenses to academic goals and objectives, as well as to the rights of fellow students." It states the reason these rules, including the GAI ones, exist; P56 (institution-level purpose statement) fits.
units.anchor: serious offenses to academic goals and objectives, as well as to the rights
units.frag_start: the university affirms that acts of cheating

units.why: The scope clause says the policy "applies to all students of the university, graduate and undergraduate, full or part-time". This sets the scope of the GAI rules, P61.
units.anchor: applies to all students of the university, graduate and undergraduate, full or part-time
units.frag_start: This policy applies to all students

notes: Only AI-relevant provisions of a longer general academic-integrity policy were coded; non-AI mechanics (panel composition, training, records) were skipped. Sanction, hearing and appeal units are included because the policy applies them to GAI misuse via its cheating definition.
